q7.answer: The API generates the 32-byte token, puts the raw value only in the link, and stores its SHA-256 hash. It also writes the raw token, encrypted with an app key, into the email_jobs row. The email worker decrypts it to build the link, sends the mail, and deletes the job once sent. The worker drops the job without sending if it is past not_after.

q8.answer: The server hashes the token from the URL with SHA-256 and looks up the row through the unique index on token_hash. It then checks the live predicate: consumed_at IS NULL, revoked_at IS NULL and expires_at > now(). If no row matches, the expired page is shown; the GET does not write to the database.

q9.answer: There is no separate counter. The count is a query over password_resets for the user's rows with issued_at in the last hour, taken under the user's FOR UPDATE lock. Old requests drop out as time passes beyond the hour, and revoked rows still count toward the limit.

q10.answer: In the same transaction as the new insert, and before it, the request revokes every live link for the user by setting revoked_at. The user row lock taken with FOR UPDATE keeps concurrent requests from racing on this. Only links issued within an accepted request are revoked, so an over-limit request leaves the existing link alone.

q11.answer: Inside one transaction, the reset row gets consumed_at set, users.password_hash is updated, all sessions rows for the user are deleted, and the password-changed email job is inserted. The job is queued before COMMIT, so it commits or rolls back with the reset. The 302 redirect to /login happens only after the commit.

q12.answer: The submit transaction selects the row by token_hash with the live predicate and FOR UPDATE. The first submit locks it and sets consumed_at before committing. The second submit waits on the lock, then re-checks the live predicate against the committed row, finds none, and rolls back to the expired page. Only one submit can change the password.
